title: Knock Down the Banner
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: The teacher emphasizes the importance of putting teachings into practice rather than just holding onto them as abstract concepts. In a world where polarization and fear are on the rise, it's easy to get caught up in trying to impose our own moral frameworks on others, leading to division and striving. Instead, Ryushin Andrea Thach suggests embracing uncertainty and provisionality, allowing for multiple perspectives and ways of solving problems, and cultivating connection with others through active listening and understanding.

sentences.text: **Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Well, there are usually reasons we come to practice, and I think one of the reasons is to try and make sense of the world: how we respond to what's happening in the world, what's happening within ourselves, and what comes up.
That's been a lot on my mind these last several months, and it's probably been on everyone in the room's mind.
So I wanted to take a thread of last week's conversation, in which we responded as a community to the shootings in Orlando, and explore that from a different point of view.
I've also been a part of a nascent interfaith response in the Christian and, I would say, other spiritual community in Whatcom County.
It has been trying to give some reflection on how to respond to the sense of fear and polarization that's going on.
It's with those conversations in my mind and my heart that I'm offering this talk up for your consideration.
So we're going to talk about case 22 in the Mumang Khan.
I see some faces I'm not so familiar with, so I'll just say this is a collection of teaching stories gathered together in one book.
There are three such books that we use, and this is one of them.
They're meant to be stories that raise questions you can't answer out of your ordinary way of thinking about things.
Case 22 is Makashapa's Knock Down the Flagpole.
I'll read it to you, and I'll explain who the characters are in a minute so that you can see yourself in them.
*Ananda asked Makashapa, "The World Honored One transmitted the robe of gold brocade to you.
What else did he transmit to you?"
Makashapa said, "Ananda."
Ananda answered, "Yes."
Makashapa said, "Knock down the flagpole at the gate."*
That's the story.
In one sense, as you'll understand in a minute, it's a transmission story, a story about revealing the great depths of the dharma and recognizing someone as a teacher.
But it's really that we want that too.
We want Buddha's enlightenment.
In some way, that's what we're all seeking by being here: to be our own medicine and to be medicine for others.
To set the stage, Makashapa was Buddha's first dharma heir, the first person he recognized as being a full teacher.
He passed on the teaching stick, wherever it is, to him.
He was one of the ten great disciples, known most prominently for his grasp of the Vinaya, the teachings of morality.
I think it's very interesting that someone who is an expert on the rules of morality is giving this particular teaching.
In a way, he's a good teacher for our times, because some of the issues at hand we put in moral terms, and we feel very strongly about them.
He was also probably one of the most austere and driven, your prototypical "oh, I would hate to do that": living on almost nothing out in the woods for decades in order to be enlightened.
That was his practice.
Ananda was Buddha's cousin.
He became a monk at the age of twelve.
I think of him as rather innocent and earnest, a really sincere practitioner, the one who hung on Buddha's every word.
For twenty-plus years he was his attendant, the person who took care of the Buddha, the Muni, and the person who remembered every single word the Buddha ever talked.
He actually was that brilliant.
He could memorize immediately, even things that he didn't understand so well when he was a young person.
He was invited to the first council after the Buddha died, a meeting of all the enlightened disciples so that they could hear the Buddha's teaching again, remember it, and record it in some way.
He was almost not invited because he wasn't an arhat, a fully enlightened person.
He was rather shunned because he knew all this material but didn't quite get it.
Yet when he recited it, he did so with such accuracy and such dignity and magnificence that people felt like it was Buddha in the room.
So this was the sense of how much he loved the Dharma, how dearly he held it to himself, and this conundrum he had of somehow not getting it.
The gold robe: he asked Vakha Peshapa, who is the first recognized teacher, "You got the gold robe," meaning you got recognized as being the teacher.
You get a gold robe and a brown one and a stick.
"What else did he give you?
Could you please explain it to me?"
This matters so very much to him.

It's not so much the title, not that he wanted to be anyone, but he really wanted to actualize the words that he knew inside out and tried to adhere to, but didn't fully understand, or didn't think he fully understood.
In a certain way, that's kind of like us as we grapple, trying to find answers to the difficult problems in our life.
We're deeply drawn by our own sense of longing for the truth, to live our lives in a way that we feel whole and complete in, but somehow we can't quite put it together.
This is Ananda's question.
Returning to the koan, Vakha Peshapa calls his name: "Ananda."
It's rather like when Zen master Zmigen, in one of the other koans, keeps saying "Master, master" to himself: "You, hey you, don't be fooled today."
Hey you, Ananda, wake up.
And Ananda in turn just answers, "Yes."
Where did that come from?
When your name is called, you pay attention, don't you?
Knock down the flagpole.
What's the flagpole?
It's a great metaphor, isn't it, for all that we fly on our flagpole.
In the case of the koan, the flagpole sits outside the monastery, and when the teacher is about to give a great talk, the banner goes up and people know.
When the talk is done, the banner goes down.
Talk's over.
Vakha Peshapa doesn't just say take down the banner, take down the story, take down your ideas.
He says, knock it down.
Take down everything.
What's he saying?
What's that about?
Ananda, look, see.
What's really here?
The mind that does not think, the mind that does not see but really knows.
What is that mind that understands?
Ananda had his own banner, his own banner of loving the dharma and wanting to understand it in a certain kind of way.

A medicine for Ananda is another poem, written by the third Chinese ancestor, Kanshi Sousen or Zeng Song, called The Great Way Is Not Called Faith in Mind, or Trust in Mind, that a few of you in the room might know.
The opening lines are: *The great way is not difficult for those who have no preferences.
When love and hate are absent, everything is clear and undisguised.* Trust in mind, faith in mind.
Sometimes we don't like those words very much, right?
Having faith in something out there, outside of ourselves.

That trust or that faith is that inherent understanding or confidence that you have after practicing for a while, or maybe just after having some experience in your young life where you know something about how the world is in balance, something about how it's in harmony and you're in a place with it.
That's that kind of confidence.
The mind is not our usual ways of thinking, our personality or our constructs.
The mind is Buddha's mind.
The mind is that huge mind.
*The great way is not difficult.* You wonder why it's so hard, then, for you and me and for Ananda.
It's because in part we have a certain striving.
We care so deeply to understand.
We care so deeply to correct or hold that which we feel is out of place.
Whatever that truth is, it might be the well-being of our family, their safety, their livelihood, our future.
It might be the stewardship of the earth, our personal freedoms or civil rights.
That thing that we hold so deeply, we strive to help.
And then after striving after it, it's rather like chasing a feather with a fan.
You push it further and further away when you do that, because the way to do it becomes less and less clear.

The great effort that you make in practice, because you have to make some kind of practice, you have to set your intention on something and aim for it, that great effort is by holding that in your heart and letting it go.
Holding your heart open, aiming at the intention.
Buddha's wisdom is found, as the Zen master Shen Yang says, in the gaps and the space in between your thoughts.

In between your very thoughts, what you understand needs to be done, how to respond, how to take care of things comes to you, not after deliberation, not after making lists and trying to figure it out.
It arises naturally out of your intention, and the effort behind that intention to try and realize the way.
The way is effortless.
The years and years of practice make us accident prone, and that understanding is almost an accident.
It comes to us like serendipity.
*The great way is not difficult for those who have no preferences.* Well, of course we have preferences.
So what does this mean?
You want to know whether your next car is going to be white or brown, whether your shoes are going to be leather or nylon, what career you're going to take.
All of that is based on our preferences.
Preferences in and of themselves are not wrong.
They're not bad.
They're actually neutral.
They don't have any moral value.
Our preferences become an issue when we attach our sense of right or wrong, good or bad, more or less to them.

But in and of themselves they are just, as the dictionary says, a liking, a partiality, a projection, a proclivity, a fondness, a taste, an inclination, a leaning, a bias, a bent, a penchant, or a predisposition.
We all have predispositions.
It's nothing more than that.
So what's the problem?
The problem is when we mistake our preferences for the truth.
We mistake them as something that has to be, the only way.
So the Chinese ancestor Kanshi Soshin says, *When love and hate are absent, everything is clear and undisguised.* Love and hate also arise.
In a certain way there's nothing wrong with them, because they're basic human emotions.
Of course they will arise.
The problem comes again when we think of them as right or wrong, or better or worse.
The problem comes when we set one against the other, when we create a love and a hate.
You see, he says "when love and hate," not love or hate.
He says when they're both absent, because it takes that duality, it takes those two things together, to make the problem.
In fact, indeed, we can't always judge what's good or bad, what's right or wrong.
They're provisional and open to the circumstance.
What seems good now may not be good a year from now in a slightly different setting.
But in setting up a duality we're trying to create our vexations, particularly when things are so uncomfortable and so overwhelming.
There are topics that deeply trouble us, whether it's gun violence, restrictions on freedoms, the right to marriage, challenges to our cultural identities, all of that.
We have such strong feelings that we want to create this and that.
And we set up those opposites when they don't exist, because actually they're different points of view of the same piece.
They're all points of view of the same piece.
The desire for safety, the need for respect, to make family and community: they're all born of the same human fabric of existence.
And so when we set them apart, when we try and divide them, we miss the truth that they're all part of the same thing.
We miss information that we need in order to see clearly.
We can't act skillfully.
We can't act in wholesome ways unless we see the whole thing skillfully.
Later on in this long poem, The Faith and Mind, the author goes on to say, *To live in the great way is neither easy nor difficult.* [unclear: "That both in it does it."] It's got uncertainty.
What's harder in uncertain times than uncertainty, right?
It's provisional.
It's changing, not fixed.
You mean there's no set answer that I can adhere to in these difficult, changing, fearful times?
And it's unknown.
It's unknown, because I can't know everything that each of you thinks about what's important and valuable.
We were talking in this interfaith conference about how difficult it was to build bridges with some of the more conservative faith communities in the county, and not knowing how to reach out.
And then we said, well, why don't we sit down and just ask them?
How do they feel about these things?
How are they responding?
What are the questions that come up in their community?
Maybe we'd learn something better about what we need to do if we were able to do that.
Even the great slogan that we made for a banner that we will carry, "Let love be our legacy."
Sounds pretty nice, doesn't it?
Probably most people can get behind that, but that's our idea.
I don't know.
*To live in the great way is neither easy nor difficult, but those of the limited views are fearful and irresolute.* Sound familiar?
Fearful, or maybe trying to sound resolute.
We fear what is outside of ourselves because we see it as such.
We see the experience of others as outside of ourselves instead of understanding that it's part of ourselves.
We feel uncertain or unsure of our actions because we see this or that, our way or that way.
We don't know what to do, or we don't believe, we get caught.
Another translation of these lines is *The great way is broad.* Isn't that wonderful?
The great way contains so much.
It's broad.
It has many answers.
It has many ways of solving problems if you allow it to be.
Neither easy nor difficult.
It's in there somewhere if you're willing to open your mind and really bear with the uncertainty, the unknown, the provisionality.
*With narrow views and doubts, your haste will slow you down.* We're quick to want to resolve the difficulty and dissonance in difficult times.
All that does is trip us up.
*Even to get caught by the idea of enlightenment is to go astray.* It's a nondual predicament.
Even in that, subject and object seem outside of themselves.
Enlightenment seems like something there instead of something here, something you can trust.
You can trust your own experience.
You can trust your own mind when you open yourself up and really listen to what's happening from that place that understands connection.
You can trust that.
"Ananda."
"Yes."
Knock down the flagpole.
Ananda, wake up.
You already have it.
You already see.
Let go of your ideas.
Yes, the immediate answer.
I'll show up.
I'm showing up.
Knock down the flagpole.
You've done your ideas.
Let go.
You're already there.
Transmission is complete.
So that's what I have to say.

I don't know if any thoughts or questions or comments come up relative to this or anything that's been on your mind, but I want to encourage you to push forth with whatever questions or doubts you have, or what you've been thinking about in the last weeks, even if it doesn't seem directly related to this.
Please.
It's Whatcom County, yes.
I don't know that it has a particular name.
It's a group of ministers and pastors from around the county who just were interested.
I can let people know that you're interested in it.
There'll be plenty to do.
Orlando.
The group had been, I think, actually responding to the increasing political polarization, the increasing sense of polarization around us.
We see it in the news.
We see it in how our Congress is acting.
We feel it maybe in the county.
And I think hearing that and feeling the suffering in their communities, people wanted to try and have a way to reach out and open a dialogue between each other.
**Participant:** We need to impose a letter to the people saying, don't try to do what Trump does.
Acknowledge it.
If he does it, don't fire back at him.
It has to be a way to both acknowledge what he's doing and not do it too.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Well, I think you're pointing to part of where I'm pointing to, which is how uncomfortable the sense of polarization is, how much it cuts us off from ourselves.
And that's what's so painful.
Way back in the sixties, it was a pretty divided Congress, and yet somehow the Great Society acts went through: Medicare, Medicaid, civil rights, education reform, integration.
All kinds of things happened in the sixties, which was a time of great divide in the Congress.
And that's because people understood that we were part of the same fabric of society.
So I would challenge us.
I challenge myself.

When things come on the radio that I don't like, and it happens often, whether it's genocide in Rwanda, the first Iraq war, or what I hear from whatever candidate I'm not as inclined to, who speaks in a way that's uncomfortable to me, it's so tempting to say enough.
It's really tiresome and burdensome.
And then there's also just allowing it, just watching the quality of my mind that comes up that wants to cut it out.
I'm not saying you do that all the time, but it's just: what can I learn, what can I see in my practice about what I'm pushing away?
And is there anything in there for me that I can understand more deeply?

Could I sit down, and I'm obviously more progressive in my point of view, I hope that doesn't put off anyone in the room who may not be as progressive, but could I sit down with someone who has a very conservative point of view and really ask them what matters and why they take some of the stances and have some of the points of view that I might feel very uncomfortable with?
Could I really do that with an open mind and an open heart to understand?
I think it's always been true that we build change within relationship, and we have to be willing to build relationship.
This practice is really about relationship.
This practice is all about relationship.
Yes, please.
Yes, thank you.
Thank you for that.
I do think our willingness to bear witness to our full humanity helps us accept what's happening in the world in a different way.
Bodhisattva has a thousand hands to carry a thousand handkerchiefs, because there's that much suffering in the world and we understand it as Bodhisattva.
You understand it when you see yourself as human.
**Participant:** And then also I do it for both sides, because it is holding on to you.
There are some differences, but it's much easier.
Thank you very much.
The problem is we've developed this thirty-second sound bite culture, and it's hard to sit down.
Even the first sit down is not productive.
You sit down with somebody who is different.
It takes sixteen years to develop a relationship.
It doesn't happen overnight.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** I see the truth in that.
Just a story of my own experience comes to mind.
As some of you know, I'm very chemically sensitive.
I was at a board meeting at our temple, where I come from, where I train.
I was on the board, and we were in a conversation about whether or not to give up incense.
This is minor compared to our topics, but it's to the point.
One of the board members was 100 percent against giving up incense.
They were adamant, and it was kind of nasty, actually.
I was in the room.
You can imagine, when one's own health and well-being and ability to stay doing what you love is threatened, that there's a lot of emotional charge.
I just realized that's really how they feel.
It really matters that much to them.
I guess I'll need to leave.
No emotional charge.
I dropped my idea about what needed to happen.
I think that actually had something to do with the fact that the whole conversation shifted.
Part of it is that I was willing to let go of my strong, fixed ideas, even though I was only holding them internally.
There was an opening.
I could accept theirs.
There was an opening for a different kind of conversation.
That doesn't mean we all are friends.
I've heard about it for years later from my teacher.
It did change something.
I want to say, yes, real intimacy takes a long time.
With some kind of connection, if one person is willing to disengage from the dichotomy, then there's no longer the same kind of dichotomy.
Just about out of time, maybe there's one more question or one more comment.
*[No speech transcribed from 32:55 to the end of the recording.]*
